children.text: On an Egypt trip, how you move matters as much as what you see.
Cairo
Giza
Luxor
Aswan
Abu Simbel
Hurghada

, Sharm el-Sheikh — on a map they line up in one country; on the ground the distances are real. Cairo to Luxor is about 700 km. Aswan is further south. Abu Simbel sits even further out across the desert from Aswan.

Egyptian movement mixes domestic flights, trains, sleepers, long-distance buses, private cars, ferries, and ride-hailing. The right answer is not decided by budget alone. Do you want to save time, see the landscape, avoid heat? Are you travelling with children or arriving at night? The conditions of the trip set the answer.
A good itinerary does not pick one mode. Fly where you should fly, take a boat where the river should be looked at, walk in the city, and use a good driver where needed.
Where to use domestic flights
Domestic flights can raise the quality of an Egypt trip considerably. On a short trip, avoiding flying turns sightseeing time into transfer time.

Cairo to Luxor, Cairo to Aswan, Cairo to Hurghada, Cairo to Sharm el-Sheikh are common domestic routes. Flight times themselves are short — generally one to one and a half hours. Even with airport time included, they are much easier than long-distance road.

Abu Simbel becomes a flight candidate too when time matters. By road from Aswan it is an early-morning, long day; by air the load is smaller. Frequency and operating days shift by season — confirm early.

Domestic flights belong on short trips, hot-season trips, trips with older travellers or children, and trips combining the Red Sea and the Nile in one go. Looked at on price alone, trains and buses look cheaper; a lost day is part of the cost too.
South by train

Trains from Cairo to Luxor and Aswan are one of the characteristically Egyptian forms of movement. Running south along the Nile valley, you see fields, villages, palm groves, and the boundary with the desert from the window.
Daytime trains suit travellers who want the landscape. They take time; for trips not in a hurry, they are worth taking once.

The sleeper train suits travellers who want to move at night. The dedicated sleeper service from Cairo to Luxor and Aswan can include dinner and breakfast. Today, instructions often point to Cairo's Upper Egypt Station — Bashteel — rather than the older Ramses Station. Confirm the departure station when booking.

The sleeper is not the cheapest option. It can run at or above a domestic flight. The value is not low price; it is moving at night and the experience itself. Leaving Cairo in the evening and arriving in Luxor or Aswan in the morning — when that flow fits the trip, it works.

You may hear an old story that foreigners can't use normal trains. In fact, foreigners do use Egyptian trains. Booking, ticket classes, and station guidance change; confirm current official or trusted booking information.
Long-distance buses
Long-distance buses are widely used from Cairo to the Red Sea, Sinai, and
Alexandria
. Companies such as Go Bus, Blue Bus, and SuperJet run air-conditioned coaches.
Buses are cheap and frequent. Cairo to Hurghada, Cairo to Sharm el-Sheikh, and Cairo to Alexandria are realistic choices.
The ride is long. Roads to the Red Sea and Sinai stretch out and the scenery becomes monotonous. On a short trip wanting to save transfer time, domestic flights can be better.

Night buses save budget but cost arrival fatigue. Arriving early and packing sites or sea straight in makes the first day heavy. For families with children or older travellers especially, don't force a night bus.
Cairo city movement
Cairo is large and traffic-heavy. Don't judge time by distance alone. A 10 km trip can be 20 minutes or over an hour.

The Cairo Metro is a practical option for travellers. For moving between the centre, Giza, the Coptic quarter, and downtown, it is often more stable than surface transport. Crowded, but predictable in time.
There are women-only cars. For solo women or women-only groups, use them if helpful. This is not alarmist; it is a practical option Cairo provides.

Ride-hailing apps are very useful in Cairo. With visible fares and destination input, language and bargaining are lighter. At airports, hotels, and big sites, pickup points can be hard to find; check the in-app meeting point.
If you take a regular taxi, use the meter or set the price before riding. Don't negotiate after arrival. This applies across Egypt, not just Cairo.
Going to Giza and Saqqara
The Giza pyramids are easiest by car from central Cairo. You can combine the metro and a taxi, but for first travellers, a hotel arrangement, ride-hailing, or a private car is easier.

For Saqqara, Dahshur, and Memphis, a private car is essentially required. They are not casual public-transport runs from central Cairo. Arrange a good driver for half a day or a day; set destinations, waiting time, and fare in advance.

Around Giza, camels, carriages, photos, and informal guiding will all be offered. If you use any of them as transport, confirm total, time, and destination before mounting. Starting in ambiguity tends to end in extra-charge conversations.
Luxor movement
Luxor is much easier to move in than Cairo. The east bank holds
Luxor Temple
, Karnak, hotels, restaurants, and the station. A lot of the centre is walkable; short transfers are easy by taxi.

To the west bank, you cross the Nile. The public ferry is cheap and used by locals — practical. Looking at Luxor Temple and the Corniche from the river is beautiful; the transfer itself is part of the trip.
To tour the west-bank sites, arrange a driver for half a day or a day. The
Valley of the Kings
, Hatshepsut,
Medinet Habu
the Colossi of Memnon
, and
Deir el-Medina
are not walkable distances. Set destinations and fare in advance; confirm there are no unnecessary souvenir-shop stops.
Carriages are common in Luxor. As short sightseeing they can be fun; confirm before riding whether the price is per carriage or per person, the time, and the route.
Aswan movement
Aswan is slower than Cairo or Luxor. Stay at a riverside hotel and you can enjoy the Corniche and the souk on foot.

For Philae, you drive to the boat dock and take a boat from there. Boat fares change with negotiation and arrangement — confirm in advance. The pricing thinks differently for a group boat and a private one.
For
Elephantine Island
and the Nubian villages, use ferries and motorboats. In Aswan, river movement is part of the town. Don't treat it as transit; treat it as time to look at the view.

A felucca is a particularly Aswan experience. An hour or two on the Nile by sail in the evening is worth it alone. Before departure, set the fare, time, and route. Even if told "pay what you like afterwards," settle a guideline first.
For Abu Simbel, road or flight. Road means an early-morning start and several hours each way. The flight is easier but depends on schedules. Either way, hold a clear day in Aswan for it.
Alexandria
From Cairo to Alexandria, the train is the natural choice. It reaches a station near the centre and suits day trips or one-night stays. Time varies by train class — confirm at booking.
In Alexandria, ride-hailing and taxis are practical. Sights spread along the coastal Corniche, and what looks close on a map can take time on foot.
There is a tram too. For visitors it is less an efficient mode of transport and more a way of seeing the city's life. With time to spare it is interesting; on a tight day, take a car.
Red Sea and Sinai
Hurghada,
Marsa Alam
, Sharm el-Sheikh, and
Dahab
sit on different transport axes from the Nile valley. They are not easily connected by rail.

Hurghada is reachable from Cairo by domestic flight or long-distance bus. You can also drive from Luxor — about three and a half to four hours. To combine the Red Sea with Luxor, Hurghada, Soma Bay, or Sahl Hasheesh are easier.

Sharm el-Sheikh from Cairo is generally by air. Bus exists but is long. Reach Dahab from Sharm by car. For Sinai's interior or the St. Catherine area, confirm road conditions, security information, and site opening status close to the visit.
In resort areas, hotel transfers and taxis dominate. For the airport-to-hotel run, confirm at booking whether the transfer is included.
When a private car is the right tool
In Egypt, a private car is practical, not a luxury, in several situations.
Touring Giza, Saqqara, and Dahshur in a day.
Working the Luxor west bank efficiently.
Combining Philae,
the Unfinished Obelisk
, and the High Dam in Aswan.
Moving from Luxor to Hurghada.
Airport transfers on early flights or late arrivals.
Going into the desert or the oases.
Stitching cheap modes together loses to a trusted driver in these cases. Confirm price in advance, what is included, waiting time, parking, and how tips are handled.
Solo women travellers and movement
Solo women travel in Egypt. Many use the metro, ride-hailing, trains, and domestic flights.
Late-night movement, low-traffic areas, and bargained taxis call for more care. In Cairo, ride-hailing, hotel cars, and the metro women-only cars reduce load.
Modest dress in cities and at religious sites reduces unwanted attention. Not limiting freedom — practical judgment to make the trip easier.
If you receive an unwanted approach, don't explain at length; decline briefly and move on. Comfort in movement isn't only the mode — it includes the judgment to switch the situation early.
Carry small notes
For Egyptian movement, small notes are very useful. Ferries, short taxis, restrooms, tips, baggage help, local transport — having only large bills makes it awkward.
When you receive large bills at the airport or hotel, break them early. Keep small notes in a separate pocket so payment and tipping go short.
Before paying, confirm currency and denomination. Before you're used to Egyptian pounds, notes can be misread. Check change on the spot too. Not rudeness; ordinary self-management.
How to combine
For a first Egypt trip, the framing organises easily:
In Cairo, mix metro, ride-hailing, and private car.
For Giza, Saqqara, and Dahshur, private car.
Cairo to Luxor or Aswan: short trip — domestic flight; experience-led — train or sleeper.
Luxor west bank: ferry and private car, or a driver-included vehicle from the start.
Luxor to Aswan: Nile cruise, dahabiya, train, or car.
Aswan to Abu Simbel: flight or early-morning road.
If the Red Sea is in: Hurghada from Luxor by car; Sharm and Marsa Alam mainly by domestic flight.
In Egypt, the cheapest transfer is not always the best. The fastest is not always the best. Decide first where in the trip you want to spend time.
Get the movement right and Egypt becomes much easier to see. Get it wrong and even the best sites sink into the fatigue. So don't leave transport for last in an Egypt trip.

deck: A practical guide to moving inside Egypt — domestic flights, trains, sleepers, long-distance buses, the Cairo metro, and Luxor and Aswan transfers.
